doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Sight reading and the Chicago big band led by Harold Fox
summary: He was never a fast reader; in a Chicago rehearsal big band with Gene Ammons and Lee Konitz he read arrangements from many famous bands.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Did you ever have occasion in those situations where someone would bring in a four page piece of music for the piano player, and you’re going “oh God, where’s the chord symbols?”

Oh, I feel the same way. I was never a fast sight reader. But you know as a kid I learned how to read music but it’s something that, you have to keep doing it. Once you stop, you’re going to not do it as well. And I stopped for years, because I went to the small band type way of playing. My reading was probably best right after high school and my first year of Roosevelt College. I was with this local big band, the one I was talking about that Gene Ammons played in. It was like the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band of today. All the heavyweights were in the band. Lee Konitz was in the band also. And we rehearsed more than we worked. We rehearsed every week on a certain day, I think it was a Wednesday or Thursday we’d get together, and the leader was a guy that passed away last year, named Harold Fox. He was a trumpet player and his family owned a tailoring business that outfitted every band just about in the country. And so Harold more or less took over I think after his father passed or retired, Harold took over the store, and Harold knew all the band leaders then. And he was trading them suits or uniforms to outfit the band, for arrangements out of their books. People like Woody Herman, Stan Kenton, some of Lionel Hampton’s book, even the Billy Eckstine Big Band. And Dizzy’s big band. We had every big band. We had a book that thick of these great arrangements. So I was in that band, and you know they had these long sheets like that, but the music was so good that it encouraged me to read music. But after that I never played in a big band again until Dizzy’s band. I was on some record dates where they had these long sheets, but record dates, fortunately for the piano player and the guitar player, they wrote mostly just chord changes, which is much easier to read than when the music is spelled out.
